What are beadsprites?

Beadsprites are a form of pixel art, most often made from "fuse beads". "Beadsprite" typically refers to recreations of characters and items (sprites) from 8-bit and 16-bit video games, but really anything goes whether it's from a video game, a portrait, or a famous piece of art, or even an entirely original piece of work created specifically for this purpose. They can range in size from just a couple inches to several feet across and using any color you can find a bead for.

What are fuse beads?

Fuse beads are small plastic tubes roughly half a centimeter long. Generally considered a kids' craft, fuse beads are placed together on a pegboard in a given pattern, then ironed so that they melt down slightly and fuse together. There are four main brands:

  • Perler - The most well-known brand in the US
  • Hama - This brand comes from Denmark
  • Nabbi - Also called PhotoPearl, this brand is Swedish
  • Artkal - One of the newest brands, Artkal is based in China

Each brand has a wide range of colors, some similar and some very different. There are other brands out there, but in most people's experience everything else is much lower quality. The brands can be mixed and matched to get the specific colors you need, but some brands don't melt with each other very well, so it's generally better to limit the mixing as much as possible.

What supplies are needed?

  • Beads
  • Pegboard(s) - these come in several different shapes and sizes, but most people prefer the simple 29x29 interlocking pegboards from Perler
  • Ironing Paper or Parchment Paper - Perler sells specialized "Ironing Paper", but most people prefer to use simple Parchment paper. It usually works better, is cheaper, and doesn't have creases from being folded if you buy it on a roll.
  • An Iron - Any standard clothing iron should work
  • Masking Tape - technically optional, but highly recommended. Check the Masking Tape Method to see why.

Check this post for suggestions on where to get beads and pegboards. Parchment paper and masking tape can be found at any grocery store and you should be able to find an iron at any general store. These can also be found online, of course.

How do you make a beadsprite?

Here's the basics:

  1. Find an image you would like to craft. You can attempt to freehand it or you can use any of several different programs to create a pattern. These patterns are basically just pixelated versions of the image.
  2. Place beads on a pegboard to recreate the image. Typically, each bead will represent one pixel of the image, so this process is pretty simple, but can take quite a while depending on the size of the image.
  3. Use the "Masking Tape Method" or simply cover the beads on the pegboard with parchment paper.
  4. Iron the beads until they fuse together. The parchment paper will prevent the beads from sticking to the iron.
  5. Let the sprite cool for a bit, then remove it from the pegboard (if it's still on one).
  6. Place a flat, somewhat heavy object on top of the sprite and let it cool completely. This will help prevent the sprite from warping as it cools.
  7. If you want to increase the stability of the sprite, you can iron the back after it has cooled enough. If you do, be sure to let it cool under something heavy against, as this side will tend to warp, as well.

Where can you get design ideas?

You can make a beadsprite from anything, really, just like painting or drawing. If you have a digital image you can use various programs to automatically create a pattern from it. Depending on the size of an image, you may also be able to simply zoom in until you can see the individual pixels, as beadsprites are perfect for pixelated images. Video game sprites from the 8-bit and 16-bit eras tend to make excellent patterns without any manipulation at all. Check here for some helpful links to get you started.

How can you make patterns from regular images?

There are several programs you can use to convert any image into a pixelated form to use as a pattern. Some were created specifically for making beadsprites, while others just happen to work very well for this purpose. See this post for links to some helpful software.

You can also use many general purpose image manipulation programs that you may already be comfortable with. Paint works well for smaller images if you can guesstimate the colors you need. If you zoom in enough, you can often get the gridlines to perfectly line up with the individual pixels. Photoshop and similar programs can help you determine the colors you'll need. I'm sure there are other programs out there that I don't know about that work, as well.

Don't forget to post your completed work here in /v/beadsprites so we can all enjoy it.

Happy beading!
